<document>
<title>Tulip</title>
<fragment>

**Tulips** are spring-blooming perennial herbaceous bulbiferous geophytes (having bulbs as storage organs) in the **Tulipa** genus. Their flowers are usually large, showy, and brightly coloured, generally red, orange, pink, yellow, or white (usually in warm colours). They often have a different coloured blotch at the base of the tepals (petals and sepals, collectively), internally. Because of a degree of variability within the populations and a long history of cultivation, classification has been complex and controversial. The tulip is a member of the lily family, Liliaceae,[1] along with 14 other genera, where it is most closely related to *Amana*, *Erythronium*, and *Gagea* in the tribe Lilieae. 


</fragment>
<fragment>
The tulip's flowers are usually large and are actinomorphic (radially symmetric) and hermaphrodite (contain both male (androecium) and female (gynoecium) characteristics), generally erect, or more rarely pendulous, and are arranged more usually as a single terminal flower, or when pluriflor as two to three (e.g. *Tulipa turkestanica*), but up to four, flowers on the end of a floriferous stem (scape), which is single arising from amongst the basal leaf rosette. In structure, the flower is generally cup or star-shaped. As with other members of Liliaceae the perianth is undifferentiated (perigonium) and biseriate (two whorled), formed from six free (i.e. apotepalous) caducous tepals arranged into two separate whorls of three parts (trimerous) each. The two whorls represent three petals and three sepals, but are termed tepals because they are nearly identical. 
</fragment>
<fragment>

Because tulip bulbs don't reliably come back every year, tulip varieties that fall out of favour with present aesthetic values have traditionally gone extinct. Unlike other flowers that do not suffer this same limitation, the Tulip's historical forms do not survive alongside their modern incarnations.[3]



### Horticultural classification[edit]


![](image)'Gavota', a division 3 cultivar
![](image)'Yonina', a division 6 cultivar
![](image)'Texas Flame', a division 10 cultivar
In horticulture, tulips are divided into fifteen groups (Divisions) mostly based on flower morphology and plant size.[52][53]




</fragment>
<fragment>
* **Div. 14: Greigii** – Scarlet flowers 15 cm (6 inches) across, on 15-centimetre (6 in) stems. Foliage mottled with brown.[55]
* **Div. 15: Species or Botanical** – The terms "species tulips" and "botanical tulips" refer to wild species in contrast to hybridised varieties.[56] As a group they have been described as being less ostentatious but more reliably vigorous as they age.[57][58]
* **Div. 16: Multiflowering** – not an official division, these tulips belong in the first 15 divisions but are often listed separately because they have multiple blooms per bulb.


They may also be classified by their flowering season:[59]



* Early flowering: Single Early Tulips, Double Early Tulips, Greigii Tulips, Kaufmanniana Tulips, Fosteriana Tulips, § Species tulips
* Mid-season flowering: Darwin Hybrid Tulips, Triumph Tulips, Parrot Tulips
* Late season flowering: Single Late Tulips, Double Late Tulips, Viridiflora Tulips, Lily-flowering Tulips, Fringed (Crispa) Tulips, Rembrandt Tulips


#### Neo-tulipae[edit]


</fragment>

Below is a quick‑reference table that matches the most‑commonly‑forced spring‑flowering bulbs (the ones growers typically “force” in a greenhouse or indoor forcing box) with the botanical family to which each belongs.  
The families follow the current APG IV classification (the system used by most modern horticultural references).

| Forced bulb (common name) | Typical cultivated species / cultivar group | Botanical family (APG IV) | Brief note on the family |
|---------------------------|--------------------------------------------|---------------------------|--------------------------|
| **Tulip** | *Tulipa* spp. (e.g., *T. gesneriana*) | **Liliaceae** | The “true lily” family; includes *Lilium*, *Erythronium*, *Gagea* and related genera. |
| **Hyacinth** | *Hyacinthus orientalis* (garden hyacinth) | **Asparagaceae** – subfamily **Scilloideae** | Formerly placed in Hyacinthaceae; now a subfamily of Asparagaceae (the asparagus family). |
| **Daffodil / Narcissus** | *Narcissus* spp. (e.g., ‘King Alfred’, ‘Dutch Golden’) | **Amaryllidaceae** – subfamily **Amaryllidoideae** | Includes *Amaryllis*, *Clivia*, *Hippeastrum* and other bulbous “amaryllis‑type” plants. |
| **Snowdrop** | *Galanthus* spp. (e.g., *G. nivalis*) | **Amaryllidaceae** – subfamily **Amaryllidoideae** | Snowdrops are closely allied with daffodils; both sit in Amaryllidaceae. |
| **Crocus** | *Crocus* spp. (e.g., *C. vernus*, *C. sativus* – saffron) | **Iridaceae** – subfamily **Iridoideae** | The iris family; many ornamental and economically important bulbous genera. |
| **Gladiolus** | *Gladiolus* spp. (e.g., ‘Grandiflorus’, ‘Giant’) | **Iridaceae** – subfamily **Iridoideae** | Also a member of the iris family, but in a different tribe (Gladioleae). |
| **Fritillaria** | *Fritillaria* spp. (e.g., *F. meleagris*) | **Liliaceae** | A “lily‑type” genus retained in Liliaceae after recent re‑arrangements. |
| **Muscari (Grape Hyacinth)** | *Muscari* spp. (e.g., *M. armeniacum*) | **Asparagaceae** – subfamily **Scilloideae** | Shares the same subfamily as true hyacinths. |
| **Scilla (Bluebell)** | *Scilla* spp. (e.g., *S. siberica*) | **Asparagaceae** – subfamily **Scilloideae** | Another Scilloideae genus, often forced for early spring color. |
| **Amaryllis (Belladonna Lily)** | *Amaryllis belladonna* | **Amaryllidaceae** – subfamily **Amaryllidoideae** | True amaryllis, distinct from *Hippeastrum* (often called “amaryllis” in the trade). |
| **Iris (Bearded, Dutch, etc.)** | *Iris* spp. (bulbous groups such as *I. reticulata*) | **Iridaceae** – subfamily **Iridoideae** | Bulbous irises are forced similarly to crocuses and gladioli. |
| **Allium (Onion, Ornamental)** | *Allium* spp. (e.g., *A. ‘Purple Sensation’*) | **Amaryllidaceae** – subfamily **Allioideae** | Formerly in Liliaceae; now placed in Amaryllidaceae. |
| **Lily (true lily)** | *Lilium* spp. (e.g., *L. ‘Stargazer’*) | **Liliaceae** | The classic “lily” family; many true lilies can be forced, though they are a bit slower than the smaller bulbs. |

### How to use the table
* **Identify the bulb you’re forcing** – look for the common name or the Latin genus/species if you know it.  
* **Check the family column** – this tells you the larger taxonomic group.  
* **Why the family matters** – bulbs in the same family often share similar cultural requirements (soil type, temperature range, watering regime, pest/disease profile). Knowing the family can help you apply a single set of cultural guidelines to several different forced bulbs at once.

### Quick “family‑by‑family” cultural tip‑sheet
| Family | Typical forcing temperature (°C) | Light requirement | Typical forcing time |
|--------|--------------------------------|-------------------|----------------------|
| **Liliaceae** | 12‑15 °C (55‑60 °F) | Bright indirect light; some direct morning sun | 8‑12 weeks |
| **Asparagaceae (Scilloideae)** | 10‑13 °C (50‑55 °F) | Bright indirect light; avoid strong direct sun | 6‑10 weeks |
| **Amaryllidaceae** | 13‑16 °C (55‑60 °F) | Bright indirect light; can tolerate a few hours of direct sun | 8‑12 weeks |
| **Iridaceae** | 12‑15 °C (55‑60 °F) | Bright light; can handle full sun if temperature stays moderate | 8‑12 weeks |

These temperature ranges are a **starting point**; many growers fine‑tune them based on the specific species or cultivar they are forcing.  

---

**Bottom line:**  
Every forced bulb belongs to one of four main families—**Liliaceae, Asparagaceae, Amaryllidaceae, or Iridaceae**—with a few sub‑family exceptions (Allioideae for *Allium*). Knowing the family helps you group bulbs with similar requirements and achieve reliable, repeatable forcing results.
